questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I've been to Norway before on vacation and loved it. I also have friends and connections in Norway which I knew prior to my arrival on exchange.
I wanted to live and study in a country that is similar to Denmark i.e. not too much of a culture shock. Norway is a beautiful country with opportunities for hiking, skiing and other experiences in nature which are not possible in Denmark in the same way.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. In the beginning the University of Oslo had an orientation week which covered all the basics. This is ranged from navigating the course registration to extracurricular activities and life in Oslo itself. The university website also provides a lot of useful information but it can be a bit information dense.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not need assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I was pleasantly surprised at how much the host university cared about our arrival and wellbeing. On the first day of the orientation week, everyone was asked individually if they had arrived safe and sound and had found housing. In case someone hadn't found housing, the host university would help them find housing as soon as possible.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: In my experience it was very easy to find housing, provided you apply for housing in good time. The main student organization SiO provides housing (among other things) to exchange students if they study at one of the main higher education institutions in Oslo. My housing application deadline was the 1st of June, so I had plenty of time to look into the different housing options and set my preferences on the website accordingly. One thing that is hard to plan for is that furnished rooms are in short supply; you only get one offer and it might be unfurnished. I had to buy temporary furniture and then sell it again at the end of the stay.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Students in Oslo live in so called "Studentbyer" or Student Towns. These large collections of buildings essentially form a small town of their own and will often have their own supermarkets, gyms, restaurants and other facilities. Many things are arranged by SiO. For example, SiO offers gym memberships at their gym chain Athletica at very student friendly prices. In general, Oslo is very well connected by a dense public transportation network consisting of metro lines, buses and trams. It only took me 15 minutes to get to campus directly with the metro line which had a station right at my student town.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It would be nice if more furnished rooms were available. They are not a guarantee.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It is a chaotic system. There are limited spots for each course and the deadlines are very late. As a result you don't know if you received a spot on a course until after the semester has already begun. I did not get into 2 out of my 3 applied courses and had to hastily apply for new courses. Luckily the student help/information office moves quickly during the course registration time. I learned that a lot of the Norwegian students apply for 10+ courses at a time for each semester and then drop out of the ones they are unable/unwilling to attend. This is one possible workaround for the current system so you can ensure you have enough courses to cover all 30 necessary credits for the exchange semester. But naturally this further exacerbates the problem. As an exchange student, you must be extra careful to select courses that do not have conflicting time schedules. There is no handy way/system to do this; you must go to every course web page and manually check that their time tables do not conflict. This is because most students at the university follow set study tracks (that do not have conflicting courses), but as an exchange student you are wholly responsible for figuring this out yourself.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Student Information office was incredibly helpful. They have office/telephone hours and usually reply to e-mails quickly. They helped me quickly select and apply for new courses with empty slots.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Initially I only got into 1 out of 3 courses I applied for. But I ended up being quite happy with my final set of courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be aware that you might not get into the courses you initially wanted. Make sure that the time tables of the courses do not conflict.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Compared to UCPH, the level of the courses is not as high. The courses take less of your time and a lot of material is a bit easier to understand. This meant that I had more free time to do other things besides studying. There are not as many mandatory assignments or weekly exercises and there is less reading material in general.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The overall structure and style is very similar to UCPH. Some reading material, some lectures and mandatory assignments which must be passed to qualify for the exam. However, some courses do not have exercise classes at all. I was not used to this, since almost all classes at my institute at UCPH have had weekly exercise classes.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Natural Language Processing
Artificial Intelligence in Energy Informatics
Advanced Database Systems for Big Data

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All courses were pretty good, but I thoroughly enjoyed and learned a lot from Natural Language Processing in particular. Besides computers, I have always had an interest in language, so to see computer science and linguistics combined in this way was very interesting.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had to furnish my room myself. Even though I bought everything second hand, this was still relatively expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food was more expensive. Groceries cost more in general, especially meat and fresh produce. Going out for dinner and drinks in town is incredibly expensive. Especially the drinks part. 

Public transport is much cheaper than in Copenhagen if you're a student. A monthly fee of around 284 DKK a month and you can get in and around every part of Oslo. 

I did not need to spend money on books. All course materials were published in the course pages of my courses. Depending on what you're studying, you might be just as fortunate, otherwise expect more spending in this category.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a large number of student organizations and activities to join, including student-run bars, sports/outdoors clubs (river rafting, hiking) or social gaming/quiz nights.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely join the first couple of quiz nights for international students during and after the orientation week. It is a great way to get to know other international students!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: If possible go on hiking trips or visit other cities/towns in Norway. I and some other exchange students went to visit Bergen by train, which was a really fun trip.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, since Denmark and Norway are quite similar culturally. I had no trouble reading and understanding Norwegian as a Dane, but your mileage may vary depending on the languages you speak.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: This part can be a bit tricky, since Norwegians can take a bit to warm up to you (as a generalization). Just try to join activities and clubs and you will probably find people you click with, but it will take some time. Classes and group work can also be good ways to meet people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There were no particularly challenging cultural differences.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: In general, Norwegians are kind and honest people. Also their Taco Friday tradition is great!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be open-minded. Going on exchange was a different sort of experience than I thought it would be, but that isn't a bad thing. Your expectations might be different from reality, so just try to keep an open mind. 

Don't be afraid to reach out to people or ask for help! If you ever need help or someone to talk to, there is always someone to talk to. Whether it be the study information office or your fellow students. 

Prioritize fun things and new experiences. Time is short. Your exchange stay will fly by. Use the time to do things you want to do!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring warm clothes and ski clothes if that is your thing. It might get cold and snowy in late fall/early winter!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Going on exchange really helped me get out of my comfort zone and grow as a person. At times it can feel demanding or scary, but I also learned how to deal with a new life situation. I now know that wherever I decide to go, I'll figure something out. It has also been very rewarding to meet all kinds of new people that I wouldn't have met otherwise and I've had experiences that I otherwise wouldn't have had.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Probably arriving all alone in an empty room and not knowing a single person in the city on the very first day. It is an incredibly humbling experience. My first thought upon arrival was: "What did I just do?!" Luckily, this feeling is only temporary. Once the semester starts and you begin meeting people, the feeling goes away.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
